children.prompt: Find the gradient, which is the constant of variation $k$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}k&=\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}\\&=\frac{3-0}{2-0}\\&=1.5\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt: What does $k$ represent in this context?

answer.worked: The cost per pack is $\$1.50$.

children.prompt: Write the equation relating $P$ and $N$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}P&=kN\\P&=1.5N\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt: Find the cost of 9 packs of pens.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=1.5(9)\\P&=13.5\end{aligned}$$
The cost is $\$13.50$.

children.prompt: How many packs can be bought for $\$27$?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}27&=1.5N\\N&=\frac{27}{1.5}\\N&=18\end{aligned}$$
18 packs can be bought.

children.prompt: Find the gradient, the constant of variation $k$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}k&=\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}\\&=\frac{180-0}{2-0}\\&=90\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt: What does $k$ represent in this context?

children.prompt: Write an equation relating $d$ and $t$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}d&=kt\\d&=90t\end{aligned}$$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}1260&=90t\\t&=\frac{1260}{90}\\t&=14\end{aligned}$$
The journey takes 14 hours.

content.prompt:
Centimetres and inches are directly proportional.
Use the graph to do these conversions:

spec.description: Unshaded conversion graph with positive-axis arrows, grey grid, black axes and labels, and one blue model series. Horizontal grid interval 1 inch; vertical grid interval 5 centimetres. The source red series is mapped to house blue.
spec.mathematics: C = 2.5I for 0 ≤ I ≤ 15. Horizontal range 0–15, labelled 0, 5, 10, 15; vertical range 0–40, labelled 10, 20, 30, 40 with a shared origin zero. The line ends at (15, 37.5), without point markers or a line arrow.
spec.answerVisibility: The supplied conversion model is permanently visible; no response answers appear in the graph.

children.label: a
children.prompt: 6 inches to cm.

answer.worked: Read up from 6 inches to the line, then across to the centimetres axis: 15 cm.

children.label: b
children.prompt: 20 cm to inches.

answer.worked: Read across from 20 cm to the line, then down to the inches axis: 8 inches.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the gradient, use the point $(10,25)$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: What does the gradient represent?

answer.worked: Each increase of 1 inch corresponds to an increase of 2.5 cm. The gradient is the conversion factor, 2.5 cm per inch.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Write an equation relating centimetres and inches. Using your equation, how many inches is 200 cm?

answer.worked:
Let $C$ be the number of centimetres and $I$ the number of inches.
$$\begin{align*}C&=2.5I\\200&=2.5I\\I&=\frac{200}{2.5}\\I&=80\end{align*}$$
200 cm is 80 inches according to the graph's model.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Convert 10 gallons to litres.

answer.worked: Reading the graph at 10 gallons gives 45 litres.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Convert 30 litres to gallons.

answer.worked: Read across from 30 litres to the line, then down to the gallons axis: approximately 6.6 gallons.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Why might your answer to part b be inaccurate?

answer.worked: The intersection lies between grid lines, so the number of gallons must be estimated from the graph.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the value of $k$ by using the point $(10,45)$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}k&=\frac{45}{10}\\k&=4.5\end{align*}$$
The conversion factor is 4.5 litres per gallon.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Hence use your equation to find the exact number of gallons for 30 litres.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}L&=4.5G\\30&=4.5G\\G&=\frac{30}{4.5}\\G&=\frac{20}{3}=6.\dot{6}\end{align*}$$
The exact number is $6.\dot{6}$ gallons.

content.prompt: Exchange A and Exchange B convert Australian dollars to US dollars. The graph shows the amount received at each exchange.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the gradient of each line.

answer.worked:
Exchange A, using $(200,120)$:
$$\begin{align*}m&=\frac{120}{200}\\m&=0.6\end{align*}$$
Exchange B, using $(200,140)$:
$$\begin{align*}m&=\frac{140}{200}\\m&=0.7\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Which exchange gives more US dollars for each Australian dollar? Explain.

answer.short: Exchange B, because its gradient is greater.
answer.worked: The gradient is the number of US dollars received per Australian dollar. Exchange B gives US$0.70 per A$1 and Exchange A gives US$0.60 per A$1, so Exchange B gives more.

children.label: c
children.prompt: How many more US dollars does Exchange B give than Exchange A for $\$150$ Australian?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Exchange A}&=0.6\times150=90\\\text{Exchange B}&=0.7\times150=105\\\text{Difference}&=105-90=15\end{align*}$$
Exchange B gives US$15 more.

classification.difficultyReason: Two gradients, a comparison with justification, and a difference of two converted amounts.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use the graph to estimate the number of cups in 700 mL.

answer.worked: Read across from 700 mL to the line, then down to the cups axis. The reading lies between 2.5 and 3 cups, at approximately 2.8 cups.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Write an equation relating the volume $V$ mL and the number of cups $c$. Using your equation, find the exact number of cups in 180 mL.

answer.worked:
The line passes through $(2,500)$.
$$\begin{align*}k&=\frac{500}{2}\\k&=250\\V&=250c\\180&=250c\\c&=\frac{180}{250}\\c&=0.72\end{align*}$$
180 mL is 0.72 cups.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the gradient of the graph and state what it represents.

answer.short: $0.4$; pounds received per Australian dollar (£0.40 for A$1).
answer.worked:
The line passes through $(150,60)$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Gradient}&=\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}\\&=\frac{60}{150}\\&=0.4\end{align*}$$
The gradient is pounds divided by Australian dollars, so A$1 converts to £0.40.

children.label: b

children.label: c
children.prompt: Explain why your answer to part b is not the gradient of this graph.

content.prompt:
The exchange rates are $\mathrm{A}\$1=\mathrm{US}\$0.65$ and $\mathrm{A}\$1=$ €$0.60$.

How many euros is $\$260$ US?

answer.worked:
Let $A$ be Australian dollars, $U$ US dollars and $E$ euros.
$$\begin{align*}U&=0.65A\\260&=0.65A\\A&=\frac{260}{0.65}\\A&=400\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}E&=0.6A\\E&=0.6\times400\\E&=240\end{align*}$$
240 euros.

classification.difficultyReason: No graph or direct rate is supplied for US dollars to euros. The student must see that the conversion goes through Australian dollars: divide 260 by 0.65 to get A$400, then multiply by 0.6. This is two linked steps with a direction decision (divide, then multiply) and some decimal arithmetic. That is more than the signposted single-rate work in p9-q6. It is less than the open-ended listing and optimising in A4.

Let $A$ be Australian dollars, $U$ US dollars and $P$ pounds.
$$\begin{align*}U&=0.64A\\320&=0.64A\\A&=\frac{320}{0.64}\\A&=500\end{align*}$$

Let $A$ be Australian dollars, $U$ US dollars and $P$ pounds.

$$\begin{align*}U&=0.64A\\U&=0.64\times312.5\\U&=200\end{align*}$$
$\$200$ US.

content.prompt:
Paul rents a guesthouse from the landlord for $\$720$ per week.

To save money, he has other people stay and divides the expense equally.

The equation that models this situation is $C = \frac{720}{n}$, where $C$ is cost in dollars per person and $n$ is the number of people staying per week.

spec.sourceRegion: Upper guesthouse activity, graph at left
spec.description: First-quadrant reciprocal curve with continuation arrows, positive-axis arrows, labelled integer horizontal ticks, labelled hundreds vertically, and half-unit/50-dollar minor grids. Axis titles are outside the ticks.
spec.mathematics: C = 720/n; displayed horizontal range 0 to 8 and vertical range 0 to 800. The continuous curve illustrates the reciprocal relationship; contextual admissible values of n are positive whole numbers.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent supplied graph; contains no part answers.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What is the cost per person when 3 people are staying?

answer.worked:
$\begin{aligned} C &= \frac{720}{3} \\ C &= 240 \end{aligned}$

The cost is $\$240$ per person.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many people are needed so cost per person is $\$144$?

answer.worked:
$\begin{aligned} 144 &= \frac{720}{n} \\ n &= \frac{720}{144} \\ n &= 5 \end{aligned}$

5 people are needed.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What are the limitations of this model? (hint: can $n$ be a fraction?)

answer.short: $n \geq 1$ and must be a whole number.
answer.worked: $n \geq 1$ and must be a whole number because at least one person is staying and a fraction of a person cannot share the expense.

methods: Rearrange to find the denominator variable.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{k}{x}\\\frac14&=\frac{k}{12}\\k&=\frac14\times12\\k&=3\\y&=\frac{3}{x}\end{align*}$$

flags.note:
[Pedagogy audit v2 · Applied automatically · Definition] The phrase 'proportional decrease' is circular and gives no equation. The replacement states xy=k and y=k/x with conditions on k and x, and says that if one quantity is multiplied by n the other is divided by n.
Replacement text: Two quantities are **inversely proportional** if their product is constant: $xy=k$, or $y=\frac{k}{x}$, where $k$ is a non-zero constant and $x\ne0$.

- An **increase** in one quantity causes a decrease in the other: if one is multiplied by $n$, the other is divided by $n$.
- A **decrease** in one quantity causes an increase in the other.

The graph of inverse variation is a **hyperbola**, also called a **reciprocal relationship**.
Applied: Replacement text applied.

flags.note:
[Pedagogy audit v2 · New teaching] The inverse lesson never teaches finding k from one given pair of values, but the pool question and Q7 and Q8 all need it. Add a short worked example after the trip guided practice that substitutes a pair into y = k/x, solves for k and writes the equation.
Worked example: The time $t$ hours taken to paint a fence is inversely proportional to the number of painters $n$. It takes 6 hours when 4 painters work. Find an equation relating $t$ and $n$.
$$\begin{align*}t&=\frac{k}{n}\\6&=\frac{k}{4}\\6\times\color{#ef6068}{4}&=\frac{k}{4}\times\color{#ef6068}{4}\\k&=24\\t&=\frac{24}{n}\end{align*}$$
Guided practice:
Proposed question: Find an equation for each inverse variation.
a) The speed $s$ km/h of a cyclist is inversely proportional to the time taken $t$ hours. When $t=3$, $s=20$.
b) The cost $c$ dollars per person is inversely proportional to the number of people $n$ sharing a bill. When $n=8$, $c=7.50$.
c) $y$ varies inversely with $x$. When $x=12$, $y=\dfrac14$.
Answers: a) $s=\dfrac{60}{t}$; b) $c=\dfrac{60}{n}$; c) $y=\dfrac{3}{x}$

entries.description: Analysing Inverse Variation with Graphs

Two quantities are inversely proportional if:
• An increase in one quantity causes a proportional decrease in the other.
• A decrease in one quantity causes a proportional increase in the other.
The graph of inverse variation is a hyperbola, also called a reciprocal relationship.

y = k/x, with a left-pointing annotation arrow identifying k as the constant of proportionality. Beside the equation is an unscaled first-quadrant reciprocal curve approaching both axes, with arrowed axes labelled x and y.

entries.description: Graphs of Change

Constructing Graphs of Rates of Change
A common question can ask you to construct a graph of a changing quantity.
For questions on height increase as you pour water at a constant rate:
• Larger cross-section: Slower increase in water height.
• Smaller cross-section: Faster increase in water height.
• Consistent cross-section: Constant rate of increase in water height.

entries.description: Speed-Time Graphs
Acceleration and Deceleration

Speed is the rate of change of distance over time,
E.g. A car travelling on a highway at 90 km per h (km/h).
Acceleration is the rate of change of speed over time,
E.g. An object falling due to gravity accelerating at 9.8 metres per second, per second (m/s²).
Acceleration is the gradient of a speed-time graph.
Negative acceleration is called deceleration.
Example Calculate acceleration and deceleration from a speed-time graph
